title: Are You the Baby or the Bathwater?
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer pushes back on the edtech industry's reflexive plea to 'not throw the baby out with the bathwater' when parents scrutinize screen time. The problem: every edtech company answers yes to the standard due-diligence checklist (evidence page, teacher-support language, dashboard, standards alignment), so those questions don't distinguish quality from junk. Meyer's replacement diagnostic is belonging: after using this product for 30 minutes, do students feel more or less connected to their school, teachers, and classmates? Research shows belonging is the only significant predictor of learning in at least one battery of motivation measures, and a RAND study of personalized-learning models found decreases of up to 10% on safety and belonging indicators. A pre-publication study found teachers using a ChatGPT wrapper showed a 0.11 SD decrease in student intrinsic motivation. The final test is visiting the class—not reading a PDF—to observe whether the product enriches or erodes the relationships at the center of learning.
points: Every edtech company has an evidence page, talks a great game about supporting teachers, and provides a dashboard—so the standard checklist fails to separate baby from bathwater.
Meyer's diagnostic: after 30 minutes with a product, do students feel more or less like they belong at school—more or less known by their teachers and classmates?

Research found sense of belonging to mathematics was the only significant predictor of learning in a battery of motivation measures; RAND found personalized-learning models decreased belonging scores by up to 10%.
A pre-publication study found that when teachers used a localized ChatGPT wrapper for lesson planning and homework support, students' intrinsic motivation decreased by 0.11 SD.
The definitive test is visiting the class: would you be proud to have a parent walk in? Do students and teachers know and appreciate each other more or less after using this product?
quotes: Look: 99% of edtech companies know how to answer “yes” to all of those questions.
After using this product for 30 minutes, do students feel more or less like they belong at this school?
Belonging, for many students, predicts and is a prerequisite for learning.
they found decreases of up to 10% on questions of safety and belonging compared to national averages.

The idea that AI creates shortcuts, saves time, and avoids effort; these are all things that could be very beneficial in the professional context where you want to maximize efficiency. But they are very, very damaging in the educational context, when the whole point is to do things the hard way—because that’s how you learn.
Ask edtech companies for evidence, yes, but know that you need more evidence than the kind you get in a PDF. The PDF is necessary but insufficient.
